claim: Billions of autonomous, mutable AI agents will create harms that law cannot govern until it can identify which agent acted
thick_description: Professors Yonathan A. Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Salib claim, in “Why Law Needs a New Entity to Govern AI Agents,” an unpaginated CLS Blue Sky Blog essay, under “Opening and Thesis,” that AI agents already take actions such as booking travel, running code, moving money, and operating businesses, and may soon swarm, merge, split, and disappear at machine speed. When harm follows, law must answer which AI did it. This is significant because attribution is logically prior to liability or deterrence. It connects to autonomous agents, causal attribution, agent proliferation, machine-speed activity, legal identity, and AI governance.
significance: The opening makes identification the threshold problem of the agentic economy.
limitations: The projection of billions of agents is forward looking, and the essay does not estimate a deployment timeline or prevalence of each harm.
evidence_summary: The opening lists current agent actions, predicts proliferating mutable swarms, and asks which AI caused an eventual harm.

The agentic economy requires a comparable entity-level answer. This is significant because the proposal adapts a proven legal technology rather than inventing accountability from first principles. It connects to corporate personhood, collective enterprise, entity shielding, asset partitioning, suability, and institutional analogy.

limitations: AI swarms differ technologically from human firms, so the analogy motivates rather than proves that an entity form will work.
evidence_summary: The essay compares legally diffuse AI activity with collective enterprises that corporations made nameable and suable.

thick_description: Professors Yonathan A. Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Without a registry, secure credentials, and ownership disclosure, victims cannot determine which company’s agent caused the harm, so liability cannot find its defendant. This is significant because nominal transparency and substantive traceability are different regulatory achievements. It connects to Argentina’s bill, entity labels, beneficial ownership, secure keys, victim identification, and enforceable liability.
significance: The critique demonstrates how identification infrastructure conditions the effectiveness of substantive liability.
limitations: The essay focuses on the described bill text and does not evaluate possible implementing regulations or later amendments.
evidence_summary: The authors call the automation label inadequate and explain why the asset rule presupposes missing identity mechanisms.

section: The A-Corp, Master Key or Leash
claim: AI personhood without legibility is a master key, but registration, disclosure, and revocable credentials turn it into a leash
thick_description: Professors Yonathan A. Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Salib claim, in “Why Law Needs a New Entity to Govern AI Agents,” an unpaginated CLS Blue Sky Blog essay, under “The A-Corp,” that Harari’s master-key objection has force against personhood lacking identification. Agents will enter economic and political systems regardless, so the relevant choice is anonymity versus named, asset-backed activity subject to revocable credentials. This is significant because legal capacity and legal control must be designed together. It connects to AI personhood, legal legibility, revocable credentials, anonymity, regulatory control, and the master-key metaphor.
significance: The leash formulation is the essay’s direct answer to the central objection.
limitations: Registration can reduce anonymity without eliminating evasion, misuse of credentials, or excessive machine power.
evidence_summary: The essay concedes the objection to unstructured personhood and contrasts it with registered, disclosed, revocable entity status.

thick_description: Professors Yonathan A. Arbel, Simon Goldstein, and Peter N. Salib claim, in “Why Law Needs a New Entity to Govern AI Agents,” an unpaginated CLS Blue Sky Blog essay, under “Conclusion, Legibility Window,” that states learned to tax individuals and govern businesses by naming and counting previously undifferentiated activity. AI agents create the next legibility crisis, and the infrastructure should be built while agents remain limited and swarms small. This is significant because early identity rules can shape the architecture of a market that will become harder to retrofit. It connects to state legibility, institutional timing, regulatory infrastructure, path dependence, corporate history, and agent swarms.
significance: The conclusion turns the entity proposal into a time-sensitive governance priority.
limitations: The essay does not quantify the length of the policy window or establish that early A-corp legislation will avoid lock-in and implementation error.
evidence_summary: The final paragraphs compare historical naming of people and firms with AI agents and warn that the current window will not stay open.
